posts: This is a card sort, so it lives or dies on the preparation. Print it, cut it, separate the piles before the lesson, and let students physically move a card when someone changes their mind.
The examples sit close to the line on purpose. If every card sorts cleanly in two minutes, the class has stopped reading them and started guessing at a pattern.
Which card split your students most evenly, and what was the argument they made for the side you did not expect?
Did you run this before or after your first big assignment of the term, and would you swap the order next time?
The eight situations are ordinary on purpose. Nothing here is a crisis, which is the point, because the ordinary ones are the responses you make fifty times a week without thinking.
Read the reasoning even when you picked the response it calls best. The why is where the transfer happens, and skipping it turns the whole thing into a quiz about your instincts.
Which of the eight did you get wrong, and did you agree with the explanation once you had read it through?
Was there a situation where your answer would change depending on the time of year? Say which one and why.
Four directions, and none of them is the safe one. The value is noticing which direction you reach for by default, because that habit turns up in every hard conversation you have.
People pick the direct route in the game and the avoidant one in real life. If those two answers differ for you, that gap is worth more than the result.
Which direction did you choose, and would you still choose it if the other person were someone you have to work beside daily?
What conversation are you currently avoiding, and which of the four directions do you think would actually move it forward?
It is a budget, so the interesting part is what you refuse to fund. Spending all hundred points on things that genuinely matter still leaves you at zero by lunch.
Build the day you actually had last week, not the ideal one. An honest budget shows you the leak, and a flattering one just shows you your good intentions.
What did you cut first when the points ran out, and was that honestly the right thing to be cutting?
Which part of your day costs far more energy than it looks like it should from the outside?
Level 2 is the trap because it sounds supportive. Warm, specific about effort, and completely silent on what the student should do next, which is the gap most of us live in.
Rate a few lines of your own recent comments before you look at the scale. Scoring someone else's writing is easy, and scoring your own is the part that changes anything.
What did you score on the first round, and which level did you find hardest to tell apart from its neighbour?
Post a piece of feedback you would rate a 4, with the student details stripped out. Curious what other people think makes it hold up.
The silly rounds are not filler. Getting the shape of Notice, Name, Next Step into your mouth on nonsense is what makes it available when a real child is standing in front of you.
Next Step is where most attempts collapse. People write a second Notice, dress it up as advice, and the learner still walks away with nothing to do differently.
Which of the three parts do you drop first when you are tired, and has naming it out loud made you any more likely to keep it?
What was the funniest thing you generated on a silly round, and did the real round land harder because of it?
The clock exists so you stop polishing. Real feedback gets written in the last four minutes of a lesson, not on a quiet evening, so the pressure is the realistic part.
Read the context before the terrible comment, not after. Half of these makeovers are impossible until you know what the learner was actually asked to do.
Did the timer help you or wreck you? Curious whether people write better feedback under pressure or considerably worse.
Which of the starting comments was closest to something you have genuinely written on a piece of work, and what was missing from it?
Twelve things, room for eight, so this is really an argument about what you believe week one is for. The four you drop say more than the eight you keep.
Worth replaying as the person you were in your first year and again as you are now. The two sets of eight rarely match, and the difference is the actual lesson.
Which four did you cut, and was there one you dropped that you would fight to keep if the list allowed nine?
For anyone further along in this work, what made your week one list shrink over the years, and what survived every cut?
Ten scenarios, and several have no clean answer, which is deliberate. Run it as a discussion rather than a score sheet or you will spend the lesson defending an answer key.
Decide where your own line sits before you hand this out. Students will ask what counts in your class specifically, and the quiz will not settle that for you.
Which scenario did your class disagree with you on, and did you move your position at all afterwards?
Did you use this to open a conversation about rules or to close one? Interested in which worked better.
The para side is written without flinching, including the moments where the second adult is handed a job and no context. Reading both columns of the same scene in order is the whole point.
Teachers tend to read their own side and nod. Do the other one slowly, because the friction in this partnership is almost always about information nobody thought to pass on.
Paras, which scene felt closest to your week, and what would you have wanted the teacher side to say?
Teachers, did anything on the para side change how you plan to hand a group over, or did it mostly confirm what you already do?
Nine months, four demands each, and you only ever get to properly attend to two. Watching the unattended ones stack up in the later months is the part that makes people go quiet.
Play it once picking whatever feels urgent, then again picking what you said mattered back in August. The second run tends to end somewhere very different.
Which month did your version fall apart in, and does that match the month it usually goes wrong in real life?
What is the one demand you deliberately let go of all year, and looking back, did letting it go actually cost you anything?
These are the calls that land between other things, with an incomplete picture and somebody waiting in the doorway. The scenarios keep that pressure instead of handing you a tidy file to read.
Useful for people who are not leaders too. Making ten of these calls in a row explains a great deal about why the answer you wanted last term never arrived.
Which scenario did you find you had no instinct for at all, and who would you have rung before deciding?
Leaders, which of the ten lands on your desk most often in real life, and does the game version get it right?
Four tasks is small enough that you cannot hide behind volume. Ranking forces you to say out loud that something genuinely comes last, which is the bit most to do lists quietly avoid.
The comparison afterwards is the useful half. Experienced educators are not ranking by urgency, they are ranking by what breaks if it slips, and that shift can be learned.
Where did your ranking differ most from the group, and did you change your mind after seeing theirs?
What is the task you rank last every single time and never actually get to? Wondering if it is the same one for everybody.
Harder than it reads. The urge to explain arrives about three turns in, and catching yourself halfway through a sentence is the entire skill being trained here.
This is not a game about clever questions. Short and plain beats elaborate, and most people lose by asking something that is advice with a question mark stuck on the end.
How many turns did you last before you gave in and told instead of asked, and what could you not resist explaining?
What is the one question you fall back on when your mind goes blank and you need to keep someone talking rather than fixing it for them?
Two minutes is the constraint that makes it usable. Anything longer becomes a thing you schedule, which means a thing you skip on exactly the days you needed it.
Take the category you land on rather than spinning again for one you like the look of. The one you keep dodging is generally the one worth two minutes.
Which category do you land on most, and which one do you quietly respin before anyone notices? The dodged one is usually the telling one.
Where in your building do you actually manage two uninterrupted minutes, and does it involve hiding? Genuinely after ideas here.
The feedback versus praise pile is where it bites. Plenty of items sound like feedback, do nothing a learner can act on, and belong firmly on the other side.
Go slowly on the proactive versus reactive set. Several items flip category depending on when you do them, and arguing with the answer is more useful than agreeing with it.
Which item did you place wrong and still think you were right about? Say which category you would move it to and why.
If you were building a third round, which pair of categories would you add? Plenty worth sorting beyond these two.
A command in a question costume is still a command, and learners hear the difference long before they can name it. This one trains the ear rather than the phrasing.
Expect to score worse than you assumed going in. Most of us carry a handful of phrases that end in a question mark and leave nobody any real choice.
Which of your own regular phrases turned out to be a command in disguise, and have you found a version that offers a real choice?
Do you think there is a place where the disguised version is the right call, or should it always be one or the other?
The guilt is built into the scenarios deliberately. A boundary you feel fine about was never the hard one, so the discomfort here is the thing actually being practised.
Notice which situations you would hold a line on for a colleague and fold on for yourself. That asymmetry shows up fast once you have worked through a few.
Which situation would you find hardest to hold in real life, and is it harder with a colleague, a parent or a leader?
What is one boundary you set this year that actually stuck, and what made it survive past the first genuinely busy week?
There is no scoring, which irritates some people and is exactly right. The information is in the split, because seeing a colleague pick the other approach makes you say why you picked yours.
Answer quickly. Deliberating turns it into a test of what you think you should say, and the fast answer sits much closer to how you actually run a room.
Which pairing did you find genuinely close to a coin toss, and what would tip you one way or the other on a given day?
Which answer left you in the minority, and did seeing the split make you rethink it or dig in harder?
Three choices, and none of them is the one you would make with unlimited time. That constraint is the realistic part, because the real version of these moments lasts about four seconds.
Worth replaying with a different room in mind. The best move with a small group is often the worst one with thirty, and the scenarios hold up under both readings.
Which scenario made you want a fourth option, and what would that option have been? Say it, the gaps are interesting.
Did your choices change between a first and second run through, and if so, was it the scenario or your mood that shifted?
The honest answer to several of these is that you should just solve it yourself. The game is about knowing which wall is worth another person's time, not about using everything on offer.
Pay attention to the scenarios where the answer is a tool rather than a person. Those are the ones people get wrong in both directions, waiting on a human or hunting alone for hours.
What have you hit a wall on recently that it never occurred to you to ask about? Worth saying out loud, others are probably stuck on the same thing.
Which scenario had your instinct saying do it yourself while the game pointed elsewhere, and who do you think was right?
